The Government of Vietnam Proposes a Pilot Visa for Remote Workers

Minister of Culture, Sports and Tourism Lam Thi Phuong Thanh presented a draft resolution on special mechanisms and policies for tourism development to the National Assembly. The draft proposes a controlled pilot program for foreigners working remotely in Vietnam. It also includes more flexible visa and residency conditions for medical tourists and individuals coming for long-term treatment, rehabilitation, or relaxation, along with accompanying family members.

The proposal aims to attract higher-spending tourists and strengthen the competitiveness of the tourism industry. The draft includes the expansion of bilateral visa-free regimes for key markets and a more flexible visa policy prioritizing high-income, long-stay, and repeat visitors, as well as conference participants. The government also proposes simplifying the issuance of work permits, visas, and temporary residence for foreign experts and artists involved in tourism projects.

The pilot program for remote workers has not yet been adopted. The Culture and Social Affairs Committee of the National Assembly, while assessing the project, noted that the resolution should not establish specific visa rules for separate groups and called for further clarification on the novelty, features, and boundaries of the proposed special visa policy. Specific rules, fees, and application procedures for the pilot visa have not been established. Remote workers will continue to use the standard electronic visa valid for up to 90 days.

📌 Clipboard Hijacking: Why the Address You Paste May Not Be Yours

Main Points
⏺ Crypto addresses are long, so almost everyone copies and pastes them
⏺ Clipboard malware watches for that moment and swaps in the attacker's address
⏺ This post explains how the swap works and the simple habit that stops it


1⃣ Core Idea — A clipper is malware that monitors your clipboard. When it sees something that looks like a wallet address, it silently replaces it with one controlled by the attacker.
2⃣ Why It Works — People check the first few and last few characters at most. Some clippers even pick look-alike addresses that match those characters.
3⃣ Example — You copy an exchange deposit address, paste it into your wallet, and hit send. The pasted address is different, and the transfer cannot be reversed.
4⃣ Risk Surface — Pirated software, fake wallet apps, cracked games and shady browser add-ons are common carriers. The malware can sit unnoticed for months.
5⃣ Practical Rule — After pasting, compare the full address with the source, or verify it on your hardware wallet screen. For new addresses, send a small test first.
Final Thoughts

The blockchain did exactly what you told it to do — the problem happened on your device before you clicked send. A ten-second check is cheaper than any lost transfer.

Omri Segev Moyal, an Israeli cybersecurity expert on X:

Well, today both Apple and the NSA’s classified network went down. Yesterday, it was Chase and United. On Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration grounded flights across the United States, and the day before that, Outlook went down for three days. Six organizations in six days, and everyone is asking who is attacking America.

My answer, as of this evening: probably no one.

That may sound strange coming from someone whose job is to investigate attacks, so let’s look at what was actually reported.

Microsoft: a bug introduced into the code in July that slipped through every test. It sat quietly for four months, until a busy day came along and more than 80% of the servers stopped responding.

The FAA: five hours without departures and more than 9,000 canceled flights. According to reports, the routers that failed dated back to 2001–2006. One administration official says new security updates overwhelmed them. Another says a contractor was in the middle of switching from copper to fiber. Two versions, the same story: someone touched something that had been left alone for 20 years.

Chase: a bug. United: according to the pilots’ union, the system that calculates weight and balance went down. Apple: an “internal update.” And at the NSA, according to reports, the network went down during routine updates, and employees were asked to stagger their arrival times so they would not all log in at once.

None of the six is pointing to an attacker. All are pointing to a change.

Could one of these eventually turn out to have been an attack? Yes. Investigations are ongoing, and if the picture changes, I’ll be the first to write about it here. Right now, there isn’t a single report establishing that.

So why is everyone convinced these are cyberattacks? Because that’s how the news works. One incident doesn’t make a pattern. Once there are two, everyone starts chasing every outage. Since Friday, every malfunction has become “another one in the wave,” and our brains fill in the rest: if there’s a wave, someone must be causing it.

I think there is a wave. Just not a wave of attacks.

Every large organization runs systems dating back to the 2000s, and the same rule applies to all of them: if it works, don’t touch it. Everyone knew they needed replacing, but no one got the budget.

Then AI arrived. Suddenly, every management team has an AI plan, complete with a budget and a deadline. And it turns out you can’t connect an AI agent to a system running on copper, with its data locked inside a 20-year-old computer. So everything that was postponed for 20 years is now being squeezed into a single work plan. All at once.

AI is also speeding everything up. Code is being written faster than a human can read it. Vulnerabilities are being discovered at an unprecedented pace, so security updates are being released at an unprecedented pace, too. But the testing team is still the same size, and the people who understood the old system retired long ago.

Not a cyberattack. A cyber rush.

None of the six has blamed AI, and Microsoft explicitly stated that its outage was unrelated to AI tools. I’m not claiming a model wrote their bug. I’m arguing that this revolution is setting the pace at which everyone is now making changes to their infrastructure, and that this is the simplest explanation for this week. My assessment, not a finding.

What should you do? Treat every upgrade as a threat. Make sure you have a way to roll back, and that you have actually tested it. Deploy to a small subset of servers first, even when the deadline is looming. And find someone who still remembers how the old system works before touching it.

When the next outage happens, before asking who attacked, ask what changed.

Nationwide FAA Ground Stop Throws U.S. Air Travel Into Chaos: More Than 12,000 Flights Canceled


A major technical disruption brought air travel across the United States to a standstill on November 13, after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered an unprecedented nationwide ground stop because of problems affecting its air traffic control communications network.

The disruption began at approximately 3:30 p.m. Eastern Time and affected 17 of the country’s 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers. Airlines were forced to suspend departures while aviation authorities worked to stabilize the system.

The scale of the disruption was significant. According to the FAA, approximately 12,462 flights were canceled on Friday, including more than 9,000 cancellations by major airlines. 

Additional delays and cancellations continued over the weekend as carriers struggled to restore normal schedules.

The agency said legacy telecommunications equipment became unstable after an unusually high volume of data flooded its network. Investigators identified potential problems involving a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, and a communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas.

The nationwide ground stop was lifted at approximately 8:15 p.m. ET, after more than four hours. The FAA stressed that safety procedures remained in place throughout the incident and that every aircraft landed safely.

Officials have found no evidence that the disruption was caused by a cyberattack. The investigation is continuing, with particular attention focused on network equipment and maintenance procedures.

The incident has reignited concerns about America’s aging aviation infrastructure and the urgent need to modernize systems responsible for managing thousands of flights every day.

For millions of travelers, the disruption was a reminder of how quickly a technical failure can affect an entire country’s transportation network.
